targetReport.title: International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities (ISIC)
targetReport.description: The United Nations' industry classification and the acknowledged parent of most national industrial classifications, including ANZSIC and its two predecessors. Its absence from this corpus was a hole of the same shape as the missing `gasb-standards` that the associated-states pass had to fill: `naics` was present with eight inbound edges while the classification NAICS itself is aligned to was not represented at all. Adopted 1948; revisions 1 (1958), 2 (1968), 3 (1990), 3.1 (2002), 4 (2007) and 5 (endorsed 2023, publication forthcoming).
targetReport.cadence_note: Six revisions in seventy-five years. Rev. 5 was endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission at its 54th session in 2023 and, as of this session's read of the UNSD page, is 'forthcoming' in published form while being distributed as introduction, explanatory notes and structure files. releases_per_year is nominal.

release_schedule.note: ISIC has no publication calendar or fixed revision cycle. Revisions occur irregularly and infrequently (Rev.3: 1989, Rev.3.1: 2002, Rev.4: 2008, Rev.5: endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission at its 54th session in March 2023). National adaptation of Rev.5 is targeted by 2025, business register updates by 2026, and statistical program implementation from 2027, but these are implementation milestones for the already-published Rev.5, not a future release date. The UN Committee of Experts on International Statistical Classifications recommended a five-year revision cycle for ISIC/CPC (raised at the 55th Statistical Commission session, 2024), but as of the 56th session (2025) documents, this had not been formally adopted -- a new Standing Task Team on ISIC and CPC was instead tasked with developing a revision-cycle strategy proposal. No computable next revision date exists yet.

results.basis: VERIFIED DIRECTLY. Resolução CMN 5.141/2024 Art. 1º: "O índice de preços a ser adotado para fins da nova sistemática de meta para a inflação... é o Índice Nacional de Preços ao Consumidor Amplo – IPCA, calculado pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística – IBGE." The Banco Central's own historical-targets page (bcb.gov.br/controleinflacao/historicometas) confirms this is operative, not merely declaratory: it reports year-by-year compliance as "Variação do IPCA" -- the published index figures are the direct input to measuring whether the target was met.

targetReport.title: Índice Nacional de Preços ao Consumidor Amplo (IPCA)
targetReport.publisher: Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE)
targetReport.description: Official consumer price index used by the Brazilian government for inflation targeting and as the primary measure of retail inflation. Covers households with monthly income from 1 to 40 minimum wages. Monthly release covering a fixed basket of goods and services collected in major metropolitan areas and selected capitals. Current series incorporates expenditure structures from the Pesquisa de Orçamentos Familiares (POF). Closely related INPC covers the narrower 1–5 minimum-wage income range. IPCA is the reference series for monetary policy and many contractual adjustments.
targetReport.cadence_note: IBGE's own page states: "Periodicidade de divulgação: Mensal".

targetReport.description: Mid- to long-term energy policy framework adopted by Cabinet Decision in February 2025. Complements the disaster-management cluster by embedding the post-Fukushima safety-first principle into long-term energy strategy.

results.basis: VERIFIED DIRECTLY (Local Government (Rating) Act 2002, version as at 27 November 2025, read from the Parliamentary Counsel Office's own PDF replayed byte-for-byte through the Wayback `id_` endpoint because legislation.govt.nz's WAF returns HTTP 202 with zero bytes to non-browser clients; pypdf-extracted, 129 pages). The chain is entirely in statute, in four hops. s.13(3): "For the purposes of this section, the rateable value of the land— (a) must be— (i) the annual value of the land; or (ii) the capital value of the land; or (iii) the land value of the land; and (b) must be identified in the local authority's funding impact statement as the value for setting a general rate." s.5 pins each of those three to the other Act: "capital value has the meaning set out in section 2(1) of the Rating Valuations Act 1998" (identically for annual value and land value). s.27(4): "The database must include, in relation to each rating unit within the local authority's district,— (a) all information that relates to the unit that is included in the district valuation roll for the district". s.5 again: "district valuation roll means,— (a) in relation to a territorial authority, a roll prepared for a district under section 7 of the Rating Valuations Act 1998 and approved under section 11 of that Act". This is New Zealand's exact counterpart to NSW Local Government Act 1993 s.498's cross-Act citation of the Valuation of Land Act 1916.

targetReport.title: District valuation roll (general revaluation)
targetReport.publisher: New Zealand territorial authorities; certified by the Valuer-General
targetReport.description: The roll of every rating unit in a territorial authority's district, prepared and maintained under Rating Valuations Act 1998 s.7 and revalued in full at intervals of not more than three years under s.9. The rating equivalent of the Netherlands' WOZ beschikking and NSW's Valuer-General land values. Its statutory gate is unusually hard: s.11(2) forbids assessing any rate on the proposed values until the Valuer-General has certified approval of the general revaluation.
targetReport.cadence_note: Three-yearly per territorial authority (RVA 1998 s.9(1)), staggered across the 66 territorial authorities, so several fall due nationally each year.

release_schedule.note: New Zealand's district valuation roll general revaluation is not a single national event: each territorial authority (TA) revalues on its own three-yearly cycle (Rating Valuations Act 1998 / LINZ guidance: 'valuations occur at least every three years'), certified by the Valuer-General. QV (Quotable Value), which conducts most councils' revaluations, publishes a rolling implementation calendar showing which TAs are due next. The image 'Revaluation_Calendar_2026_V1.jpg' fetched from the QV schedule page on 2026-08-11 lists the current tranche of upcoming TA implementation dates, September 2026 through April 2027, soonest first. Entries below group TAs by implementation month exactly as published; only some of the ~67 TAs are shown (those in the currently-published near-term tranche).

targetReport.title: Rating Valuations Act 1998

targetReport.description: The Act creating the Valuer-General (s.3), setting the Valuer-General's standard-setting, monitoring and certification functions (s.4), empowering the Rating Valuations Rules (s.5), requiring each territorial authority to keep a district valuation roll (s.7), requiring three-yearly general revaluation (s.9) and forbidding rates to be assessed on uncertified values (s.11(2)). release_schedule.note: This corpus entry is the statute text itself (Rating Valuations Act 1998) on legislation.govt.nz. The consolidated 'as at' version is only reprinted when an amending Act or regulation takes effect — there is no periodic publication calendar or stated rule for revising/reprinting the Act's text. The current consolidated version is 'as at 23 December 2023' (last amendment date), and next reprint depends on whenever Parliament next amends it — unpredictable. Note: the Act's own Section 9 ('General revaluation of rolls at 3-yearly intervals') states that territorial authorities must generally revalue rating valuation rolls every 3 years, but that rule governs the underlying property-valuation rolls process (administered locally, staggered by council per QV's rolling revaluation calendar), not the timing of updates to this Act's text — so it isn't a valid stated-rule for this specific report/URL.

results.basis: VERIFIED DIRECTLY by this session (2026-08-06, second thread): the Act read in a browser on legislation.govt.nz, the annual report's own text extracted from the 108-page PDF at ao.parliament.nz. The report states its governing instruments in its own front matter: "The annual report informs our stakeholders – Parliament, New Zealanders, and public organisations – about our strategic intentions, priorities, and performance for the year 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025. (b) an account of the implementation of the annual plan required under section 36; and (c) a list of entities audited by the Auditor-General under an arrangement in accordance with section 19." This is methodology_depends_on rather than cites because the statute dictates the report's contents, not merely its existence. targetReport.title: Public Audit Act 2001
targetReport.publisher: Parliamentary Counsel Office (administered by the Office of the Auditor-General)
targetReport.description: The statute that constitutes the Auditor-General, defines 'public entity', and requires the annual plan (s 36) and the annual report (s 37). Minted 2026-08-06 because it was already load-bearing in this corpus without a node: XRB A1 defines 'public sector PBE' by cross-reference to it, Wellington City Council self-classifies under it, and the Tokelau audit mandate turns on it. Schedule 2, 'Specific public entities not falling within any class' (s 5(1)(d)), lists "Tokelau Administration" by name. A full-text search of the current consolidation returns one occurrence of 'Tokelau' and zero of 'Niue' — which is the sharpest single piece of evidence for the export-of-institution finding, because it shows New Zealand statute reaching into Tokelau and being silent on Niue, whose Constitution instead reaches out.
targetReport.cadence_note: A consolidated statute, reprinted on amendment rather than published on a schedule. Version read 2026-08-06 is the current consolidation on legislation.govt.nz, which carries amendments through the Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Act 2025 in Schedule 2.

release_schedule.note: This is a piece of primary legislation (Public Audit Act 2001, No 10), not a periodic statistical release. The New Zealand Legislation site republishes it as an updated 'reprint' each time an amending Act or regulation changes its text, e.g. as at 23 December 2023, 30 June 2024, 01 October 2024, 27 October 2024, 27 August 2025, and 01 January 2026. These reprint dates are driven by unpredictable parliamentary amendment activity, not by any calendar or stated periodic-review rule, and show no consistent time-of-year pattern.

results.basis: VERIFIED DIRECTLY (Public Audit Act 2001, current consolidation, legislation.govt.nz, DOM extraction against div.prov per this branch's established method, this session). s 5, interpretation, imports three defined terms wholesale by cross-reference: "Crown entity has the same meaning as in section 2(1) of the Public Finance Act 1989," "department has the same meaning as in section 2(1) of the Public Finance Act 1989," and "office of Parliament has the same meaning as in section 2(1) of the Public Finance Act 1989." s 37(1), already quoted in this slice for the annual-report edge, routes the Auditor-General's own reporting obligation through the other Act: "...must prepare and present an annual report to the House of Representatives in accordance with section 43 of the Public Finance Act 1989." PFA 1989 s 43, read directly this session, confirmed as "Departments must prepare annual reports" -- the general departmental annual-report provision the Auditor-General's own report follows. methodology_depends_on: the classification terms PAA's own scope provisions turn on (which entities are Crown entities, departments, Offices of Parliament) are defined in the other Act, not this one.
results.evidenceQuote: the Auditor-General must prepare and present an annual report to the House of Representatives in accordance with section 43 of the Public Finance Act 1989.

targetReport.title: Public Finance Act 1989
targetReport.publisher: Parliamentary Counsel Office (administered by The Treasury)
targetReport.description: The statute governing the use of Crown financial resources. Minted 2026-08-07 on Thomas's decision (planning/Decisions-2026-08-07.docx, option A: mint on arrival, and the minting session adds every edge it can verify with a direct quote in the same session, no cap, nothing minted on inference), closing a lead three prior sessions had deferred as 'probably the right next statute to mint' (NZ/G.4.md, following the Tokelau/Public Audit Act 2001 work). s 1A(1): "The purpose of this Act is to consolidate and amend the law governing the use of public financial resources." Requires the Treasury to prepare the annual consolidated Financial Statements of the Government (s 27) and the twice-yearly economic and fiscal updates (s 26O). Also supplies the other half of a bidirectional statutory cross-reference with the Public Audit Act 2001: s 2(1), "Office of Parliament means the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment (and that Commissioner's office), the Office of Ombudsmen, and the Auditor-General" -- naming the Auditor-General as one of only three Offices of Parliament this Act recognises -- and s 2(1) again, "Auditor-General has the meaning given to it by section 4 of the Public Audit Act 2001." Each Act defines a term the other Act's own scope provisions rely on.
targetReport.cadence_note: A consolidated statute, reprinted on amendment rather than published on a schedule. Version read this session (2026-08-07) is 'Latest version as at 01 July 2026', carrying amendments through the Public Finance Amendment Act 2026 (2026 No 9).

release_schedule.note: This is the Public Finance Act 1989 itself (NZ primary legislation), not a periodic statistical report. The legislation.govt.nz page is a consolidated 'reprint' that is updated only when Parliament passes an amending Act into force (currently shown 'as at 13 November 2025'). There is no published release calendar and no statutory rule specifying when the next amendment/update will occur — changes depend entirely on the parliamentary legislative agenda, so the update cadence is genuinely irregular.

results.basis: VERIFIED DIRECTLY (Public Finance Act 1989, current consolidation, legislation.govt.nz, DOM extraction against div.prov, this session). The cross-reference between these two Acts runs both ways, independently documented on each side -- see the companion edge in the opposite direction. s 2(1) interpretation: "Auditor-General has the meaning given to it by section 4 of the Public Audit Act 2001." s 29B: "the Government reporting entity is a public entity as defined in section 4 of the Public Audit Act 2001 and, in accordance with that Act, the Auditor-General is its auditor." The Government's own audit arrangement -- who audits the consolidated Financial Statements of the Government -- is assigned by PFA 1989 through a defined term the Public Audit Act 2001 supplies, not defined afresh. methodology_depends_on rather than cites: s 29B does not merely mention the Auditor-General, it assigns the audit function by operation of the other Act's own definition of 'public entity'.

targetReport.title: IMF Enhanced General Data Dissemination System (e-GDDS)
targetReport.description: The IMF's data-dissemination tier for countries not on the (stricter) SDDS/SDDS Plus standards already in the graph. Kenya implemented e-GDDS (with a National Summary Data Page) around 2018, per the IMF's own DSBB e-GDDS pages and confirmed via a related IMF press release. A notch below South Africa and Egypt, both confirmed on full SDDS -- worth having as a distinct node so the graph can actually show the tiering rather than treating every country's IMF dissemination status as equivalent.

results.basis: Article XVI §8(b)(2)-(3) makes the guarantee turn on the same per capita personal income figure that drives the Gann limit: Test 3 applies instead of Test 2 when the change in California per capita personal income exceeds the change in per capita General Fund revenues plus one-half of one percent, in which case prior-year allocations are increased by per capita General Fund revenue growth plus 0.5 percent. The "change in California per capita personal income" is the figure defined by Government Code §7901(a) and published annually by the Department of Finance as the Article XIII B price factor.
results.evidenceQuote: This paragraph shall be operative only in a fiscal year in which the percentage growth in California per capita personal income is less than or equal to the percentage growth in per capita General Fund revenues plus one half of one percent.

targetReport.title: Price Factor and Population Information (Article XIII B appropriations limit factors)
targetReport.publisher: California Department of Finance, Demographic Research Unit
targetReport.description: The annual letter transmitting to every California city and county the two factors that adjust the Article XIII B appropriations limit — the "Gann limit". Attachment A gives the price factor, the percentage change in California per capita personal income; Attachment B gives each city's and unincorporated county's population percentage change as of January 1. Revenue and Taxation Code §2227 requires transmission by May 1; the higher population estimate is certified to the State Controller by June 1.

release_schedule.rule: California Revenue and Taxation Code Section 2227: "Such statements shall be transmitted by May 1" — the Department of Finance must transmit its estimate of the percentage change in population (and, in practice, the accompanying price factor for Article XIII B appropriations limit calculations) to local agencies by May 1 each year.
